title: BCDR Tabletop, SLA & Escalation Walkthrough + Compliance Pack - Aurora Health
next_steps: Redwood to share SOC 2 Type II report, ISO summary, and sample audit logs (by 2025-08-15)
Customer to provide list of required data residency regions and legal contacts for DPA review (by 2025-08-18)
Schedule tabletop rehearse with Aurora on-call + Redwood on-call (proposed 2025-08-28)
Redwood SE to run a short failover proof-of-concept (RTO/RPO) in staging (target week of 2025-09-01)
action_items: Maya Patel: Send SOC2 Type II, ISO certs, and sample audit logs export (due 2025-08-15)
Carlos Nguyen: Draft BCDR runbook outline and share runbook template (due 2025-08-14)
Tom Reyes: Share Aurora's required RPO/RTO targets and regulated dataset inventory (due 2025-08-18)
Priya Menon: Provide legal checklist and DPA redlines (due 2025-08-22)
summary: Call focused on validating Redwood's incident response and business continuity / disaster recovery posture for Aurora Health. Discussed RTO/RPO targets, failover approaches (warm standby vs active-active), escalation paths (PagerDuty/phone/Slack + Redwood on-call), SLA language and credits, RBAC/SSO provisioning, audit log retention and exportability, and KMS/BYOK options for encryption. Agreed next steps: share SOC 2 and ISO artifacts, run a small staged failover test, and prepare a joint tabletop drill with on-call rotations.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Location: Zoom / recorded
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood SE), Dr. Leena Shah (CISO, Aurora), Tom Reyes (IT Ops Manager), Priya Menon (Head of Legal), Ben Ortiz (VP Eng)
Shared artifacts: SOC2_TypeII_Redwood_v2.pdf (link), BCDR_runbook_template.xlsx (link), SLA-draft-aurora-redwood.pdf (link)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): walking through incident response, RTO/RPO, escalation, encryption/KMS, and audit logs; questions on data residency and on-prem private deployment options.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you carving time. Quick intros? I'll kick it off. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the Aurora account, and Carlos is our systems engineer.
[00:12] Carlos Nguyen: Hey all, Carlos here, I focus on infra and resiliency, will drive the technical parts of the tabletop.
[00:18] Dr. Leena Shah: Leena, CISO Aurora, I'll lead security questions.
[00:22] Tom Reyes: Tom, IT ops, day-to-day SRE-ish for Aurora.
[00:25] Priya Menon: Priya, legal.
[00:27] Ben Ortiz: Ben, VP Eng, here for decision or timeline items.

[00:35] Maya Patel: Great. Agenda — short: confirm Aurora's RTO/RPO expectations, walk through a typical incident escalation from detection to full failover, show where Redwood's audit logs and KMS options fit, and capture any contract/SLA asks. We'll end with explicit next steps.

[00:52] Tom Reyes: Quick note — we're regulated, so data residency is huge for us. We're only allowed to keep PHI in the US and EU if applicable. So we need to confirm where logs and retention live.
[01:05] Carlos Nguyen: Totally, we can pin model serving to region and have logs retained in the same region. One nuance — some auxiliary logs (control plane) might be in Redwood's control plane region unless you choose Private deployment.
[01:23] Dr. Leena Shah: When you say control plane, do you mean audit trails for admin actions? We need those retained for at least 12 months, immutable if possible.
[01:34] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, admin audit trails and policy changes. We provide append-only audit logs with tamper-evident checksums; retention is 12 months by default and we can extend to 7 years on an add-on. The logs are exportable via secure API. (a bit garbled: "tamper-evi- e-dent checksums" in transcript)

[01:55] Priya Menon: OK can you share a sample export? We need to map fields for our e-discovery and compliance team.
[02:05] Maya Patel: We'll include sample export in the packet. Carlos, can you note that?
[02:10] Carlos Nguyen: Noted. I'll attach a sanitized logs dump.

[02:15] [02:15] Ben Ortiz: On SLA — what's the RTO we could realistically expect for a full region failover? We talked earlier about warm standby vs active-active.
[02:26] Carlos Nguyen: So typical patterns — warm standby: we maintain warm capacity in a second region, failover orchestration takes between roughly 10–30 minutes for control plane handoff plus model cold-start time depending on model size. For the smaller LMs that's sub-15, for larger LLMs, cold-start + compilation could push it toward 20–40. Our target RTO example for warm standby is 15 minutes for core endpoints; RPO depends on KV cache and prefix caching, we can get RPO down to 60–300 seconds with continuous replication, or near-zero for actively replicated state in dedicated setups.
[03:10] Dr. Leena Shah: We need RTO <= 30 minutes and RPO <= 5 minutes for our critical PHI-flows. Sounds like you can meet that with dedicated replication?
[03:22] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, with dedicated capacity and cross-region replication enabled we can get RPO under 5 minutes. We should schedule a test to validate for your specific model sizes and sequence length.

[03:38] Tom Reyes: Is that part of Redwood Dedicated or private deployment? We need to understand cost tradeoffs.
[03:45] Maya Patel: Good question — Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput; cross-region replication on Dedicated is supported. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you the most control but has higher ops overhead and licensing. We'll include pricing comparatives in the follow-up.

[04:05] [04:05] Priya Menon: On encryption — we need BYOK, HSM-backed keys, and separation of duties. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[04:15] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we support BYOK via AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and customer HSMs for private. For hosted we support envelope encryption with customer master keys; logs and data-at-rest are encrypted AES-256, control plane secrets never stored in plaintext. There's also an option for FIPS-140-2 compliant HSM usage in dedicated/private.
[04:40] Dr. Leena Shah: Are the encryption keys ever accessible to Redwood SREs? We need strict controls and proof during audits.
[04:48] Carlos Nguyen: No, with BYOK the master key is in your KMS and we never receive the key material. We have a documented KMS integration guide and can provide attestation language for audits.

[05:00] Maya Patel: (quick aside) We'll attach the KMS integration guide and a sample attestation clause for your legal team.
[05:06] Priya Menon: Please do. Also, SSO and provisioning: we use Okta and SCIM. How's RBAC handled?
[05:15] Carlos Nguyen: We integrate with SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with customizable roles scoped to org, team, and route. You can map SAML groups to roles, and we support just-in-time provisioning. There was a small typo in the transcription earlier — "R-B-ack" — but it's RBAC.

[05:36] Tom Reyes: For emergency access, do you have break-glass flows? We need auditable break-glass and temporary elevation tied to approval.
[05:45] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — temporary elevation can be done via SSO request workflows and is logged in the audit trail. We also store the approver and TTL for the elevated session.

[06:00] [06:00] Dr. Leena Shah: Let's walk incident response steps. Tom, what's Aurora's detection & triage?
[06:07] Tom Reyes: We have APM alerts, anomaly detection and security monitoring. On detection, primary SRE triages, then we escalate to the incident commander and security.
[06:15] Dr. Leena Shah: OK, for a Redwood-hosted outage, what's your typical on-call escalation and communication cadence?
[06:23] Carlos Nguyen: Redwood uses PagerDuty for real incidents. Our first-line on-call will pick up within 5 minutes, SEs are engaged, and there's a 15-minute SLA for triage acknowledgement on P1 incidents for enterprise customers. We also have an NOC runbook and an optional dedicated NOC/Pager Duty integration for critical customers.

[06:48] Maya Patel: I'll pull the P1/P2 definitions from the SLA draft and share.
[06:52] Tom Reyes: For SLA credits — how are those computed? We're sensitive to very low availability windows since we're patient-facing.
[06:59] Carlos Nguyen: SLA credits are pro-rated for downtime windows beyond the guaranteed uptime. Typically policy: 99.9% monthly uptime gives you credits tiered at 99.9/99.5/99.0 thresholds. We can discuss a custom SLA for enterprise customers with stricter targets and contractual remedies.

[07:20] [07:20] Ben Ortiz: Question — what's the communication channel during a live incident? Do you open a joint war room with Redwood? Slack bridge? Dedicated phone tree?
[07:29] Maya Patel: We offer a few options: Slack bridge (direct channel between teams), a dedicated war room (Zoom + doc), and phone escalation if it's P1. For Dedicated or Private customers we can provide dedicated Slack workspace connections and an account-specific escalation matrix.

[07:45] Tom Reyes: We'd prefer Slack bridge + phone for P1s. Also wants SLAs on time-to-acknowledge and time-to-restore.

[07:55] Carlos Nguyen: Noted. Time-to-acknowledge is 15 minutes for P1, time-to-restore is negotiated for stricter SLAs. We'll capture the target numbers in the SLA draft.

[08:08] [08:08] Priya Menon: For audits — can we get a continuous evidence feed? e.g., log exports, periodic attestations?
[08:16] Carlos Nguyen: We can provide automated log exports to your S3/Azure container, periodic attestations, and quarterly compliance reports. For high-compliance customers we also offer on-prem control plane options.

[08:30] Maya Patel: Let's pivot to tabletop. Carlos, can you run us through a P1 scenario — region outage causing degradation of inference endpoints for PHI flows.

[08:40] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. Scenario: primary region GOV-NYC goes down. Detection: Redwood health checks fail or customer alerts. Step 1: auto-detection/alert; Step 2: Redwood's first-line on-call triages — confirm outage and scope (which routes/models affected); Step 3: decide failover type — automatic to warm standby or manual failover if model verification needed; Step 4: activate failover, update routing, and notify stakeholders. Post incident: capture incident timeline, customer communication, RCA and SLA credit calculation.

[09:15] [09:15] Dr. Leena Shah: In that flow, who makes the final decision to failover? Aurora or Redwood? We need clear authorization rules.
[09:24] Carlos Nguyen: For Hosted customers, the default is Redwood can initiate automatic-failover per policy, but we always attempt to notify and get alignment. For Dedicated/Private, customers can opt to be the failover controller. We can add an authorization matrix in the runbook.

[09:44] Tom Reyes: We want a policy that Redwood holds for automatic failover only if we explicitly grant autoperm, otherwise call us first. That reduces risk of unintended promotions.

[09:55] Maya Patel: That's straight-forward; we can set the policy flag per environment.

[10:00] [10:00] Ben Ortiz: A question about cached state — KV caches and prefix caches. If we failover, is that lost? What's the wasted warm-up?
[10:10] Carlos Nguyen: Unless you have cross-region replication for caches, caches are local. We do continuous replication option for critical keys; without it, you'll see increased cold token costs and latency until cache warms. For large models cache warm-up could be tens of minutes; we can mitigate with pre-warming flows during failover.

[10:38] Tom Reyes: Pre-warming — who triggers that? Is it automatic?
[10:42] Carlos Nguyen: We can script pre-warm based on customer traffic replay or a smoke-test suite. It's configurable.

[10:50] [10:50] Priya Menon: Legal question — breach notification timelines. Aurora must receive notification within X hours for certain incidents. Can that be contractually guaranteed?

[10:58] Maya Patel: We can include contractual breach notification terms. Typical is notify within 72 hours for data breaches, but we can tighten for PHI to 24 hours as a contractual SLA. We'll need legal to agree on the exact language and triggers.

[11:12] Priya Menon: We'll propose 24-hour notification for PII/PHI exposure events.

[11:18] [11:18] Carlos Nguyen: Also worth noting — for incidents involving customer-keyed encryption (BYOK), we need customer to confirm key revocation actions; Redwood can't decrypt without customer KMS permission. So some mitigation steps require coordination.

[11:35] Dr. Leena Shah: That's fine, but we want documented runbook steps where Redwood lists which mitigation actions are customer-led vs Redwood-led.

[11:42] Maya Patel: We'll map that out in the runbook template.

[11:48] [11:48] Ben Ortiz: Regarding data residency—if we need private deployment or on-prem for PHI, what's the lead time?

[11:56] Carlos Nguyen: On-prem or air-gapped deployments are multi-week to multi-month depending on hardware procurement and networking. For VPC-hosted private deploys in a cloud region it's typically 4–8 weeks including certs, network peering and security review.

[12:14] Tom Reyes: That's OK, we have a multi-quarter plan. For near-term we'll focus on dedicated cross-region replication in US-EAST + US-WEST.

[12:24] [12:24] Maya Patel: Good. Back to SLA — do you have target uptime requirements now?

[12:28] Ben Ortiz: For critical endpoints we need 99.95% monthly uptime or better. For non-critical, 99.9% is OK.

[12:36] Carlos Nguyen: We can discuss a 99.95% custom SLA on Dedicated with penalties/credits. We'll flesh that in the SLA draft.

[12:45] [12:45] Dr. Leena Shah: A few technical clarifications — are API request logs PII-sanitized by default? If model responses could contain PHI, what logging policy applies?

[12:56] Carlos Nguyen: By default we log request metadata and request/response hashes, not full user payloads for PHI-sensitive customers. For customers that require it, we offer an option to redact or not log full payloads. There's also an explicit PII handling setting. We'll surface that in documentation.

[13:15] Tom Reyes: So if we choose no-payload-logging, does that break debugging?

[13:20] Carlos Nguyen: It makes root cause harder; usually customers enable selective sampling with strict retention. We can agree per-route sampling and sampling rates.

[13:33] [13:33] Priya Menon: On e-discovery and audits: we need immutable copies of audit logs. What's the chain of custody for those?

[13:43] Carlos Nguyen: Exports to your S3 bucket with object lock/immutability is the recommended pattern. We can also feed logs into your SIEM.

[13:50] Maya Patel: Note: we'll provide sample IAM policies for S3 export and object-lock examples.

[13:58] [13:58] Ben Ortiz: Any known limitations around model compilation time during failover if we use huge models (70B+)?

[14:05] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, compilation and kernel selection can add minutes for very large models. We mitigate with model warm-up artifacts, pre-compiled kernels, and quantization profiles. For mission-critical workloads we recommend either keeping hot replicas in standby or quantized variants to reduce cold-start.

[14:30] [14:30] Dr. Leena Shah: Let's talk forensic support — in a confirmed breach, will Redwood provide forensic logs, packet captures, and RMS timelines?

[14:41] Carlos Nguyen: We can provide forensic logs and event timeline extracts. Packet captures are available only in private deployments; for hosted we can provide connection metadata and flow logs. For deeper network captures we'd need the private deployment or joint capture with your network taps.

[14:58] Tom Reyes: Good to know.

[15:02] [15:02] Maya Patel: Quick break — we are halfway, any blockers so far?
[15:06] Dr. Leena Shah: One ask — include a sample incident communication template for regulators.

[15:12] Maya Patel: Will do.

[15:20] [15:20] Carlos Nguyen: Back to the runbook — I'm going to outline the main sections: detection, classification (P1/P2/P3), containment, mitigation, communication, failover, postmortem and SLA crediting. For each we'll list owners (Aurora vs Redwood) and automation hooks.

[15:40] Dr. Leena Shah: For classification, we will define P1 as patient-impacting PHI leakage or >5 minutes outage for critical endpoints.

[15:51] Carlos Nguyen: Understood. I'll model the runbook to that threshold.

[15:58] [15:58] Ben Ortiz: Anything about third-party sub-processors? We need a list for our supply-chain risk assessment.

[16:06] Maya Patel: We'll include the subprocessors list and the Data Processing Addendum (DPA).

[16:10] Priya Menon: Please include whether Redwood uses any offshore contractors for support or on-call. That's a deal-breaker for some of our customers.

[16:18] Carlos Nguyen: We can provide that list and, if required, restrict support to US-based teams via an enterprise package.

[16:28] [16:28] Tom Reyes: Another practical — escalations: pager -> SE -> engineering -> on-call dev. Can you map estimated time-to-engage at each tier?

[16:38] Carlos Nguyen: Typical: pager to first-line (5 min), SE engagement (15 min), engineering/subject matter (30–60 min) depending on complexity. For enterprise, guaranteed faster engage SLAs are available.

[16:55] Maya Patel: Carlos, can you provide the on-call roster cadence and the escalation phone list in the runbook?

[17:00] Carlos Nguyen: Yes. We'll redact personal numbers in the shared doc but provide role-based contacts and on-call rotation info.

[17:07] [17:07] Dr. Leena Shah: I want to flag regulatory reporting windows — certain jurisdictions require 72-hour reporting but some require 48 or 24 hours. Check the places Aurora operates.

[17:18] Tom Reyes: We'll send the list of jurisdictions and our regulator contacts.

[17:25] [17:25] Ben Ortiz: On pricing for Dedicated + cross-region replication — ballpark numbers now?

[17:32] Maya Patel: We'll follow up with a detailed pricing sheet, but ballpark is X for reserved capacity + Y for cross-region replication + optional NOC support. We'll deliver a formal quote.

[17:44] [17:44] Priya Menon: Legal: we need indemnity language for data breaches — is Redwood comfortable with standard cloud vendor terms?

[17:53] Maya Patel: We have standard indemnities; we'll surface them and willing to negotiate enterprise terms subject to risk assessment.

[18:02] [18:02] Carlos Nguyen: A technical note — for compliance we version our runbook and keep change logs; we can provide a signed snapshot for audits.

[18:10] Dr. Leena Shah: That's helpful.

[18:15] [18:15] Maya Patel: Let's do a quick mock escalation — I'll call a P1: model serving for critical endpoint degrading. Carlos, go.

[18:23] Carlos Nguyen: Ok, detection -> on-call alerted -> first triage: confirm degradation via metrics (latency/5xx); if it's region-level we declare potential failover. Step: gather model versions, traffic routing, and last successful health. If config error, rollback; if infra, assess failover.

[18:46] Tom Reyes: If it's a config error caused by Aurora change, we want immediate rollback ability. Is that supported?

[18:53] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we support route rollbacks and config snapshots. We encourage pre-approved config change windows and can pause rollout if needed.

[19:04] [19:04] Maya Patel: A note on the audit trail during this mock — every action is logged with timestamp and actor, and available in the audit export.

[19:12] Priya Menon: Will the export include the content of config diffs? We need that for compliance.

[19:18] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, diffs and previous config snapshots are included.

[19:25] [19:25] Ben Ortiz: Back to RTO/RPO numbers for our final doc — can you commit an RTO <= 30m and RPO <= 5m for critical workloads under Dedicated?

[19:35] Carlos Nguyen: We'll commit to targeting those numbers with Dedicated + replication + pre-warm, subject to successful validation during the staging failover POC. We'll make validation a gating item in the SLA.

[19:50] [19:50] Tom Reyes: Good. Also, can Redwood supply runbook playbooks we can embed into our internal PagerDuty?

[19:57] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we'll provide playbook snippets for PagerDuty runbooks and a runbook YAML that can be imported.

[20:05] [20:05] Dr. Leena Shah: Any more on encryption key lifecycle? Key rotation schedules?

[20:12] Carlos Nguyen: Key rotation is customer-managed for BYOK; for Redwood-managed keys we rotate per compliance cycles and provide rotation logs. We recommend quarterly rotation for high-security.

[20:25] Priya Menon: For legal, please add a clause that key rotation won't break historical audit exports and that old logs remain decryptable for the retention window.

[20:34] Carlos Nguyen: Affirmative — archived logs are re-encrypted but maintain decryption history as long as key is available; if you revoke key permanently, archived data becomes unrecoverable, which is expected. We'll document that.

[20:46] [20:46] Maya Patel: We're hitting review phase. Quick recap from our side and asks.

[20:52] Carlos Nguyen: Recap: 1) Redwood provides audit logs with 12-month default retention, exportable; 2) BYOK via KMS/HSM supported; 3) Dedicated supports cross-region replication to meet RPO <=5m/RTO <=30m after validation POC; 4) Escalation via PagerDuty + Slack bridge + phone; 5) Custom SLA (99.95%) possible for critical endpoints; 6) Private/on-prem options have longer lead time.

[21:25] Dr. Leena Shah: That covers most. A couple of outstanding items — PII logging defaults, breach notification time, and subprocessors list.

[21:33] Maya Patel: We'll share PII logging options, propose 24-hour breach notification for PHI, and send the subprocessors list.

[21:40] [21:40] Tom Reyes: For the POC failover test — is there a recommended test plan? We want to validate model latency/regression and cache warm-up behavior.

[21:49] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we'll provide a test plan: smoke tests, traffic replay of X QPS for 30 minutes, model correctness checks, and cache warm-up metrics. We'll include acceptance criteria.

[22:05] Priya Menon: Legal to legal — we'll need the DPA and any SOC attestations signed.

[22:12] Maya Patel: Understood. Priya, I'll send the DPA and SOC artifacts.

[22:20] [22:20] Ben Ortiz: One last operational note — we want regular joint incident drills every quarter. Is that something Redwood runs with customers?

[22:29] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, quarterly tabletop drills are recommended; we can co-run them and rotate on-call roles. We'll propose a cadence in the follow-up.

[22:40] Maya Patel: Great. We're at time. Final quick recap of action items and owners — I'll read them out.

[22:47] Maya Patel: Action 1: Maya to send SOC2 Type II, ISO summary and log export sample (due 8/15). Action 2: Carlos to draft BCDR runbook and playbook snippets (due 8/14). Action 3: Aurora (Tom) to provide RTO/RPO formal targets and regulated data inventory (due 8/18). Action 4: Priya to send legal DPA comments and breach notification requirements (due 8/22). We'll schedule the failover POC week of 9/1 and tabletop 8/28 as proposed.

[23:25] Carlos Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and the runbook outline.
[23:30] Dr. Leena Shah: Appreciate it. We'll review and come back with DPA redlines.

[23:34] Tom Reyes: Thanks, bye.
[23:36] Priya Menon: Thanks.
[23:38] Ben Ortiz: Bye.

[23:40] End call.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional word swap (e.g., "tamper-evi e-dent"), minor speaker label shifts, and some autogenerated summaries present.
